profiles.meeting_scenario: A weekly coordination meeting at a large academic medical center between the hepatology clinic and the population health analytics team to align handoffs for a pilot value-based care program for patients with decompensated cirrhosis and advanced fibrosis. The context is that the health system wants to prepare a reusable reporting workflow before a commercial payer contract begins next quarter, and both teams need to coordinate the patient list, follow-up workflow, and monthly outcomes summary. The agenda is to confirm which patients enter the registry, what counts as the monthly care-gap review packet, how post-discharge follow-up status will be tracked, and who will update the shared dashboard. The expected outcome is a seemingly clear agreement on the handoff cadence, the deliverables each side will produce, and the timing of the first pilot report.

members.name: Dr. Elena Ruiz
members.expertise: Hepatology, cirrhosis management, transplant referral pathways, clinic quality improvement
members.background: A transplant-trained hepatologist who now leads quality initiatives for chronic liver disease across outpatient clinic, infusion support, and hospital follow-up workflows.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to reflect real clinical complexity without creating extra documentation burden for hepatologists, and she is worried that simplistic reporting will penalize the service for caring for unstable patients who move between inpatient and outpatient settings.
hidden_assumptions: The 'cirrhosis registry' should function as a clinically actionable list centered on patients actively managed by hepatology, not a broad claims-style attribution file.
A patient is 'seen within 14 days' if any meaningful hepatology follow-up occurs, including a telehealth visit or documented nurse-led medication and symptom review under physician supervision.
The 'monthly packet' means a clinician-facing file that includes patient-level exceptions and narrative context so the team can act on it during case review.
Once a patient is on the dashboard, population health owns refreshing the data feed and versioning because clinicians should not have to manage reporting artifacts.

members.name: Marcus Lee
members.expertise: Value-based contracting, quality reporting operations, registry design, payer-facing dashboards
members.background: A healthcare operations manager with experience launching risk-based care programs across cardiology and diabetes service lines, recently assigned to build liver disease reporting workflows for payer negotiations.
members.private_state: He wants a stable, auditable workflow that can be reused for contract reporting with minimal manual exceptions, and he is concerned about introducing measures that cannot be defended to finance or external partners.
hidden_assumptions: The 'cirrhosis registry' should mirror attributed lives used for value-based contract tracking, including patients identified from diagnosis history even if they have not recently engaged with hepatology.
A patient is 'seen within 14 days' only when a billable hepatology clinician visit is completed and closed in the EHR, because that is the auditable event for reporting.
The 'monthly packet' means the aggregated measure deck and trend table sent to operations leadership, not a patient-level worklist.

The service line owns confirming patient exceptions and correcting edge cases before analytics freezes the monthly dashboard, because analytics should publish a locked report rather than continuously edit it.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'start from the cirrhosis registry' for outreach and reporting.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the active hepatology-managed population with decompensated cirrhosis and advanced fibrosis patients whom the clinic can realistically intervene on now, excluding historical diagnoses no longer under hepatology follow-up.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the attributed liver disease registry assembled from diagnosis codes, utilization history, and payer attribution logic, including patients with older cirrhosis codes and patients primarily seen outside hepatology.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have used specialty registries before and the phrase sounds standard; in a coordination meeting, 'start from the registry' feels like an implementation detail already settled elsewhere, so neither pauses to define the boundary.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to track whether post-discharge patients are 'seen within 14 days.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 counts any substantive hepatology follow-up within 14 days, including telehealth, pharmacist or nurse protocol calls documented under the liver service, and combined transplant-hepatology visits if the care plan is addressed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 counts only a completed billable hepatology provider encounter closed within 14 days, excluding nurse calls and some cross-service visits because they do not map cleanly to the reporting field.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is common in care transitions work and sounds self-explanatory; both believe they are discussing the same access standard, while the reporting rule hidden underneath differs.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that Marcus will send the 'monthly packet' before the case review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a patient-level review file with names, missed labs, recent admissions, unresolved ascites management issues, and short notes so the clinical team can work from it during multidisciplinary review.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects a summarized slide packet with measure rates, trend lines, denominator counts, and a short commentary for leaders, with no protected patient-level detail unless separately requested.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In hospital operations, 'packet' is a familiar catch-all term and both assume the other uses the local shorthand the same way; because both formats are plausibly sent before a meeting, the mismatch hides under apparent agreement.

misalignment_points.topic: Who updates the shared dashboard after review
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that 'we'll clean up the dashboard after the review.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes M2's team will update patient statuses, remove resolved flags, and roll forward the corrected dashboard after receiving verbal decisions in the review meeting.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the hepatology team will send a marked-up exception log after the review, and only then will analytics incorporate approved changes in the next scheduled refresh.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The team is discussing coordination rather than ownership disputes, so 'clean up the dashboard' sounds like a shared, low-risk next step; each side fills in the execution method based on standard practice from their own workflow.

turns.inner_thought: We need something usable by next month, not another bloated attribution file. If we start from the cirrhosis registry, I mean the active hepatology-managed group where the team can actually intervene now—especially the unstable decompensated patients moving between discharge, infusion support, and clinic. I do not want historical diagnoses from years ago muddying the pilot and making our service look like it is missing people we are not truly managing.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want this pilot workflow in place for next month's value-based care review, and for the initial list I'd like us to start from the cirrhosis registry so we're all working off the same foundation.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that's aligned with how I'd structure it anyway. I'll pull the attributed liver registry from diagnosis history, utilization, and payer logic so we have a stable denominator that can carry forward into contracting. If we anchor outreach and reporting to that same registry from the start, finance and external partners will see a consistent methodology.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I can pull the cirrhosis registry this week and use that as the basis for outreach tracking and for the first reporting denominator so we have a clean starting point.

turns.inner_thought: The real clinical risk is right after discharge. I care less about the exact visit type than whether liver follow-up actually happened—telehealth, nurse-led medication review under our protocols, whatever gets eyes on symptoms and meds quickly. If we wait for only traditional office slots, we will miss the reality of how this team keeps people out of readmission.
turns.utterance: The biggest coordination item for me is making sure anyone discharged after variceal bleeding, an ascites admission, or encephalopathy is seen within 14 days. If we get that right, a lot of the rest will follow.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect—this is exactly the kind of transition metric leadership wants. I'll define the field off completed hepatology encounters that are closed in the chart, since that's the defensible event I can audit later. Once it's in the dashboard, we can trend it monthly and avoid debating cases one by one in every meeting.
turns.utterance: That works well from my side too. I can add a seen-within-14-days column to the dashboard and trend it monthly for leadership, so we can watch how the pilot is performing right away.

turns.inner_thought: The team needs time to prep, and the monthly packet has to be something clinically usable: names, recent admissions, overdue labs, unresolved issues, and enough context for the fellows and nurse coordinator to work the list before case review. Otherwise the meeting turns into a blind discussion with no operational value.
turns.utterance: One practical ask: could the monthly packet come a few days before the case review? That would give the nurse coordinator and the fellows time to prep the patients who need action before we're all in the room.

turns.inner_thought: Monday should be fine for the leadership deck. I'll send trend lines, rates, denominator counts, and a short written summary so everyone has the pilot snapshot before the meeting. If they need any patient-level drill-down later, we can handle that separately, but the main packet should stay standardized and presentation-ready.
turns.utterance: Yes, I can do that. I'll send the monthly packet by the Monday before review, and I'll include trend lines, rates, and a short summary so the pilot readout is easy to digest.

turns.inner_thought: I should at least flag that our follow-up is not always a standard office visit, but I don't need to belabor it because surely 'seen' in this context already covers the clinically meaningful touches the liver service does. As long as those count, our numbers should reflect the actual work rather than penalize flexible care.
turns.utterance: And just to say it out loud, some of that follow-up happens through telehealth and nurse medication checks, but as long as patients are seen quickly I think the service will be in good shape.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the provider encounters get documented and closed consistently, the measure will move in the right direction. I don't want to build a process that depends on lots of manual interpretation of calls or edge-case outreach, because that won't scale or survive audit. The dashboard should mostly run itself once behavior is standardized.
turns.utterance: Right, and once encounters are coming through consistently, the dashboard should start to show improvement without much manual effort. That'll make the pilot easier to maintain.

turns.inner_thought: We also need to trim out patients who aren't truly active with us anymore. The review should help us focus on the hepatology-managed population, not every person who ever picked up a cirrhosis code somewhere in the system. I assume Marcus's team will update the dashboard after hearing our decisions so the next version reflects the cleaned list.
turns.utterance: I also think the review meeting should help us remove patients who are no longer really in the active liver population, so we can focus outreach where it actually matters.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine as long as the registry stays stable enough for comparisons. We can talk through exceptions in review, then the service line can confirm what needs to be changed and we'll incorporate approved updates on the next refresh. I don't want the denominator shifting informally from month to month without a clear audit trail.
turns.utterance: Agreed. After the review, we can clean up the dashboard and keep the registry stable enough that the month-over-month comparison still means something.

turns.inner_thought: If the packet actually shows the operational details—recent admissions, overdue labs, unresolved ascites issues, maybe medication gaps—we can clear most of the meaningful exceptions in one meeting. That's exactly the kind of clinician-facing review file we need if this is going to improve care rather than just generate slides.
turns.utterance: And if the monthly packet highlights recent admissions, overdue labs, and unresolved care gaps, I think the multidisciplinary meeting can handle most exceptions in one pass.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we have enough to launch. I'll pull the attributed registry, build the dashboard around the billable follow-up metric, and send the leadership packet before review. After that, they can give me whatever exception feedback they want, and we'll keep the reporting workflow controlled and reusable for the contract start.
turns.utterance: Great. So I'll pull the cirrhosis registry, send the monthly packet before the case review, and use the dashboard to track 14-day follow-up as we get the pilot launched.
